source_text: Sed quoniam unum aliquod attigimus uacuae obseruationis, non pigebit cetera quoque denotare, quibus merito uanitas exprobranda est, siquidem sine ullius aut dominici aut apostolici praecepti auctoritate fiunt. huiusmodi enim non religioni, sed superstitioni deputantur, affectata et coacta et curiosi potius quam rationalis officii, certe uel eo coercenda, quod gentilibus adaequent. ut est quorundam expositis paenulis orationem facere; sic enim adeunt ad idola nationes. quod utique si fieri oporteret, apostoli, qui de habitu orandi docent, comprehendissent; nisi si qui putant Paulum paenulam suam in oratione penes Carpum reliquisse. deus scilicet non audiat paenulatos, qui tres sanctos in fornace Babylonii regis orantes cum sarabaris et tiaris suis exaudiuit.
orientation: Tertullian is criticizing practices of prayer that have no dominical or apostolic authority, and he now gives the example of praying with cloaks laid aside.
pass_a_gloss: But since we have touched on one instance of empty observance, it will not be irksome to mark the rest also, on which vanity is deservedly to be reproached, since indeed they are done without the authority of any either dominical or apostolic precept. For things of this kind are counted not to religion but to superstition, affected and forced and of a curious rather than rational office, certainly to be restrained at least by this, that they make themselves equal to the gentiles. As it is the practice of certain people to make prayer with their cloaks laid aside; for thus do the nations approach their idols. Which certainly if it ought to be done, the apostles, who teach about the dress of praying, would have included it; unless perhaps some think that Paul left his cloak in prayer with Carpus. God, of course, would not hear those wearing cloaks, who heard the three holy men praying in the furnace of the Babylonian king with their trousers and their turbans.

choices.why: Keeps the adjective-noun force of 'uacuae' as void of authority, matching Tertullian's contrast with true religion

choices.english: counted not to religion but to superstition
choices.why: Preserves the dative of assignment and the sharp antithesis
rejected: reckoned as not religion but superstition
assigned not to religion but to superstition

choices.term: affectata et coacta et curiosi potius quam rationalis officii
choices.english: affected and forced and of a curious rather than rational office
choices.why: Keeps the threefold characterization and the genitive of quality with 'officii'
rejected: artificial and constrained and of a meddlesome rather than reasonable duty

choices.english: make themselves equal to the gentiles
choices.why: The verb is middle/passive in force; 'gentiles' is the standard term for pagans in Tertullian
rejected: put themselves on a level with the nations

choices.why: Ablative absolute; 'paenula' is a specific Roman travelling cloak, kept as 'cloak' for clarity

choices.english: with their trousers and their turbans
choices.why: Keeps the exotic Persian garments as concrete nouns, matching the Daniel 3 scene

pass_b_english: But since I have touched on one empty observance, I will not hesitate to point out the rest as well. They rightly deserve to be reproached as vanity, since they are done without the authority of any command from the Lord or the apostles. Practices of this kind are counted not to religion but to superstition. They are affected and forced, and they belong to a curious rather than a rational office. Certainly they should be restrained for this reason at least: that they make themselves equal to the gentiles. An example is the practice of some who pray with their cloaks laid aside. That is how the nations approach their idols. If this were really necessary, the apostles, who teach about the proper dress for prayer, would have included it. Unless someone thinks Paul left his cloak with Carpus during prayer. God, of course, does not hear people in cloaks. The same God heard three holy men praying in the furnace of the Babylonian king with their trousers and their turbans on (Daniel 3:21).

last_rejected.quote: that they make themselves equal to the gentiles
last_rejected.why: Subject is the practices, not the people; practices 'equal' what gentiles do.
last_rejected.fix: that they match what the gentiles do
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'quod gentilibus adaequent' means 'because they are equal to the Gentiles'; translation adds unnecessary agency but meaning remains.

polish.changed: Broke long sentences into shorter, clearer units; clarified the sarcastic point about Paul and Carpus by separating it from the preceding clause; made the final contrast about God hearing the three holy men more direct and readable aloud.

notes.quote: Paul left his cloak with Carpus
notes.why: Reference to 2 Timothy 4:13 is obscure; reader does not know who Carpus is.
notes.fix: Note: alludes to 2 Tim 4:13, where Paul asks Timothy to bring his cloak from Carpus.
